title: Saguache County Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Saguache County wells have a median depth of 120 ft. Compare local yields, water-level trends and estimated finished-well costs of $12,000-$21,000.
h1: What to Expect From a Well in Saguache County
intro_html:
A Saguache County well budget starts with the parcel, not just the county average. The recorded median depth is 120 ft, but the middle half of wells runs from 87-215 ft. That spread matters when pricing land near Center, Crestone, Moffat, Saguache or Bonanza.

Colorado DWR records contain 8,582 permits countywide, with 5,723 wells recorded as constructed. These records mix household, stock, irrigation and monitoring uses. Use the county figures to frame your questions, then check nearby completed wells and the actual permit before committing to a purchase.

sections.heading: A 120-Foot Median Is a Starting Point, Not a Bid
sections.html:
Among the 5,666 wells reporting depth, the median is 120 ft, and the middle half spans 87-215 ft. For a drilling bid, that means budgeting around a range rather than assuming the crew will stop at the median. The 90th-percentile depth is 400 ft, so deeper work is a real part of the county record.

The cost model describes mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. Permits also carry both unconfined San Luis Valley aquifer names and a large unnamed/fractured-bedrock category. That broad category does not establish the geology beneath your lot. Compare nearby logs around Moffat or Crestone with your proposed site, and ask the driller how formation changes could affect depth, casing and the final bill.

sections.heading: Saguache County Yield Records Mix Homes With Irrigation
sections.html:
The 1,698 reported pump yields have a median of 15.0 gpm, but the middle half stretches from 10.6-660.0 gpm. That unusually broad range should not be read as a household-well expectation. Irrigation appears on 30% of permits, and large-capacity wells affect the countywide picture.

The reported share under 1 gpm is 0%, while 5% falls in the 1-5 gpm band. Those figures do not guarantee that an untested parcel will produce adequately; yield is missing from many records. For an existing home, request a current pumping and recovery test. Compare household demand and any storage needs with sustained production, not simply the pump's rated capacity or an old permit entry.

sections.heading: Recorded Water Levels Have Become Deeper
sections.html:
Static water level is the resting depth to water, not the drilled depth or the level during pumping. Across 535 reporting wells, the median is 30 ft below ground, with the middle half at 15-60 ft. A shallow resting level does not mean a shallow completed well will be adequate.

The measurement-decade medians deepen from 12 ft in the 1960s to 20 ft in the 2000s, 30 ft in the 2010s and 38 ft in the 2020s. That pattern suggests declining groundwater levels in the recorded sample. It is not a repeat-measurement history of the same wells, however. Different locations and aquifers can affect the comparison. Ask for recent static and pumping levels on the property you intend to buy.

sections.heading: Permit Activity Runs Through 2026
sections.html:
Saguache County's listed permit history includes 1,576 permits in the 1990s, 1,121 in the 2000s and 911 in the 2010s. The 2020s account for 720, with the newest permit dated 2026. The current decade is incomplete, so its total is not a direct measure of slowing demand.

Leading driller entries include Valley Pump Company (Self, Clinton L.) with 357 records and American Drilling Service (Dewberry, Bradford W.) with 306. Another entry, Authorized (Pe, Pg), appears on 259; treat that as a database label rather than a confirmed contractor identity. Historical record counts do not establish current availability. When seeking bids, ask about recent work near your parcel and experience with its expected formations.

sections.heading: Budget for More Than the Saguache County Borehole
sections.html:
The supplied drilling model uses $50-$75 per foot for mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. At the 120 ft median depth, the drilled hole is approximately $6,000-$9,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at $12,000-$21,000.

Those are planning figures, not a parcel-specific quote. A deeper completion, difficult access or a long utility route can change the scope. Ask for an itemized proposal that explains casing and grout, pump selection, testing, trenching and electrical work. Also have the contractor state how additional depth and unsuccessful drilling are billed. Keep driveway construction, septic installation and broader site development separate unless the written proposal expressly includes them.

sections.heading: Check Water Quality and the Whole Building Site
sections.html:
The environmental screening data lists 6 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 41 historic mine features and 3 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites within the mapped search distance of about 10 miles. These are flags for location-specific review, not proof that a particular well is contaminated. A PFAS sampling location is not necessarily a confirmed contamination source.

Before closing, obtain laboratory testing for drinking-water suitability and discuss targeted testing with local health officials when nearby mapped features warrant it. Review casing, grout and the sanitary wellhead, too. An old yield entry cannot rule out present low production or the risk of an unsuccessful new hole. Lay out the well, septic system, replacement area, building footprint and drilling access together before fixing the house location.

sections.heading: Buying Near Center, Crestone or Bonanza: Start With the Permit
sections.html:
Start with the actual DWR permit and completion documents, then compare neighboring wells in the same local setting. Countywide averages can hide differences between parcels around Center, Crestone, Moffat, Saguache and Bonanza. Records from nearby Rio Grande or Alamosa County may add context, but they should not replace the closest relevant well logs.

Verify that the permit authorizes your intended uses. A household-use well does not automatically allow lawn irrigation, livestock watering or additional dwellings, and physical production does not establish a legal right to pump. New or expanded uses in an over-appropriated basin may require augmentation or another approved water-supply arrangement. Before buying vacant land, confirm the permitting path with DWR and have the driller and site contractor review access, utilities and septic feasibility.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Saguache County?
faq.a: The median recorded depth is 120 ft, and the middle half of reporting wells is 87-215 ft deep. The 90th-percentile depth is 400 ft. Those figures describe the county, not a guaranteed completion depth for your parcel. Nearby well logs and the formations beneath the proposed drilling location are more useful for a firm bid.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Saguache County?
faq.a: The planning model uses $50-$75 per foot. At the county's 120 ft median depth, the drilled hole is about $6,000-$9,000, while a finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $12,000-$21,000. Ask for a written scope covering casing, grout, testing and extra-depth charges rather than comparing borehole prices alone.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Saguache County?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a median of 15.0 gpm, with a middle-half range of 10.6-660.0 gpm. The records include irrigation wells, so the upper end is not a household-well benchmark. Although the reported share under 1 gpm is 0%, many permits lack yield data. Test an existing well's sustained production and recovery before relying on it.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Saguache County?
faq.a: Safety has to be established for the individual well through laboratory testing and a construction review. The mapped screening data includes 6 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 41 historic mine features and 3 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Their presence does not prove your water is affected. Use their locations to guide questions about targeted testing.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Saguache County?
faq.a: Recorded decade medians suggest deeper groundwater levels: 12 ft below ground in the 1960s, 20 ft in the 2000s and 38 ft in the 2020s. However, these are not necessarily repeated measurements from the same wells. The pattern warrants caution, but a buying decision should also use recent water-level and pumping information for the specific property.
